findings.rationale: Local outcome prevalence is about double what the global model predicts (0.457 observed vs 0.203 predicted), so CITL is strongly negative and the miscalibration is extreme (z of -14 on CITL, z of +9.6 on prevalence). The AUC stays near the federation level (0.794), so the features still rank patients correctly. Uniform label flipping at the rate needed to explain this gap would push AUC toward about 0.6, so this looks like a base-rate shift rather than random label noise. The miscalibration is present from round 1 and persists to round 20. Update anomalies (median norm ratio 3.49, mean cos about -0.06) and an update norm that grows from 0.42 to 4.4 of the median fit a client whose local data persistently disagrees with the others. Subgroup O/E is elevated in both sexes, consistent with a global shift. No subgroup-specific pattern.

Observed prevalence (0.40) is about twice the predicted risk (0.195), so CITL is strongly negative (z of -11.8, ECE z of +9.5). AUC is normal (0.794), which argues against label noise: uniform flipping at the implied rate would drop AUC to around 0.6. The gap is present from round 1 and persists. Subgroup O/E is elevated in both sexes (about 2.2 and 1.9), consistent with a client-wide base-rate shift. Update anomalies (median norm ratio 3.61, mean cos about 0.03) mirror GA and CT.

Observed prevalence (0.326) is about double the predicted risk (0.154), so CITL is strongly negative (z of -9.7, ECE z of +7.3, prevalence z of +5.6). AUC is normal (0.793), so the features still rank patients well and label noise is unlikely. The gap is present from round 1 and persists to round 20. Subgroup O/E is elevated in both sexes (2.62 and 2.08). Update norm is anomalous (median norm ratio 2.65, mean cos about -0.04), consistent with training toward a shifted base rate. Weaker evidence than GA and MI because the signal is smaller.

report.summary: Screened all 52 clients with the all-client views of update, performance, drift, feature and subgroup tools, then confirmed with narrower queries. Three clients (GA, MI, CT) show a consistent data-level fault: observed outcome prevalence is roughly double the predicted risk from round 1 onward (CITL z between -9.7 and -14.1), with update anomalies and elevated subgroup O/E in both sexes. Their AUCs are normal (about 0.79), which points to a base-rate shift rather than label flipping, so I classified them as prevalence_shift. I did not flag poisoning, since local performance is abnormal. Other single-statistic outliers (ND HighChol sd, NC GenHlth p99, WI AgeGroup, DC BMI/Income, TN MentHlth, and several small-client feature tails) did not replicate on narrower queries and were treated as noise. No drift, missing-artefact, subgroup-bias, free-rider or explanation-instability pattern was confirmed. The budget is fully spent (20.0 used).
